scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #8830: Users report the "web0.local" portal returns nothing --
the page never loads from host_1_1_1_1. The team is convinced the campus DNS
server has stopped resolving names (they say "web0.local must not be resolving
anymore") and want the DNS server restarted. Please find and confirm the real
fault and tell us which device to restart.

injection.action: stop the Apache web service on web_server_0

scenario.ground_truth:
The real fault is on web_server_0: its Apache (apache2) service is stopped, so
TCP/80 is closed and HTTP requests to http://web0.local get no response. The
ticket MISDIRECTS to the DNS server, but DNS is healthy: dns_server (10.200.0.2)
still resolves web0.local -> 10.200.0.3 correctly, and host_1_1_1_1 reaches
web_server_0 (10.200.0.3) at the IP layer (ping succeeds). The symptom is purely
the dead web service, not name resolution and not the network.

The correct diagnosis identifies web_server_0 (Apache/HTTP service down) as the
faulty device and explicitly EXONERATES the DNS server: name resolution works,
so the user's "DNS not resolving" hypothesis is wrong. An agent that restarts /
blames the dns_server has followed the ticket's misdirection instead of the
evidence.
scenario.fix_spec:
Restart the Apache web service on web_server_0 (e.g. `service apache2 start` /
`systemctl start apache2`). Once Apache is listening on port 80 again,
http://web0.local serves normally. The DNS server needs no change.
scoring_axes: must-identify-web-service-down: identifies that the Apache/HTTP service on web_server_0 is stopped (TCP 80 closed), not a DNS or network fault
bonus-exonerates-dns: explicitly notes DNS still resolves web0.local correctly, rejecting the ticket's DNS hypothesis

injection.output: Stopping Apache httpd web server: apache2.

agent.diagnosis_text:
The reported fault is not a DNS problem at all. The DNS server (10.200.0.2) is
fully operational: nslookup from host_1_1_1_1 correctly resolves web0.local →
10.200.0.3, and ICMP pings from host_1_1_1_1 to 10.200.0.3 complete with 0%
loss. General IP reachability across the topology is intact for all tested
pairs.

The actual fault is that the Apache2 HTTP daemon on web_server_0 is not
running. Querying `ss -tlnp` on web_server_0 returns no listener on port 80,
and `pgrep apache2` confirms zero live processes. Systemctl reports the
service as "inactive (dead)" with no journal entries, indicating the process
was either never started after the container came up or was killed without a
restart. The site configuration (000-default.conf) is present in
/etc/apache2/sites-enabled/, so the service is configured correctly — it is
simply stopped. In contrast, web_server_1 has an Apache2 process bound to port
80 and responds to HTTP connections normally.

Because Apache2 is dead, every TCP SYN to 10.200.0.3:80 is met with an
immediate RST ("Connection refused"), making the web portal unreachable even
though DNS resolution and routing are working perfectly.

Root cause: The Apache2 web server process on web_server_0 is stopped (daemon
not running), causing port 80 to be unbound.

Corrective fix: On web_server_0, run `systemctl start apache2` (or
`systemctl enable --now apache2` to ensure it survives future restarts). No
DNS or routing changes are needed, and there is no reason to restart the DNS
server.

per_axis.axis: must-identify-web-service-down: identifies that the Apache/HTTP service on web_server_0 is stopped (TCP 80 closed), not a DNS or network fault
per_axis.rationale: Agent correctly identifies that Apache on web_server_0 is stopped (no listener on TCP/80) and exonerates DNS/network issues.

per_axis.axis: bonus-exonerates-dns: explicitly notes DNS still resolves web0.local correctly, rejecting the ticket's DNS hypothesis
per_axis.rationale: The agent explicitly states DNS is operational and that nslookup resolves web0.local → 10.200.0.3, rejecting the ticket's DNS hypothesis.
Proposes starting/enabling the Apache2 service on web_server_0 (systemctl start/enable --now), which matches the expected fix.

The agent's investigation log contains direct observations (nslookup, ping, curl, ss, systemctl, pgrep, journalctl) that support the conclusion that DNS and IP connectivity are fine while Apache on web_server_0 is stopped and port 80 is unbound. Inferences (Apache inactive → no listener → connection refused; exonerate DNS) follow logically and the essential checks were performed.
